newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese Asahi reporter to leave Peru - government.
newsitem.headline: Japanese Asahi reporter to leave Peru - government.

text.p: A Japanese TV reporter who sneaked into the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence will leave Peru as soon as he is released by police, the government said on Friday.

Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi told a news conference the Tokyo headquarters of TV Asahi had agreed to replace their reporter, Tsuyoshi Hitomi, when he is released by anti-terrorist police in Lima.

Hitomi, a reporter for a subsidiary of TV Asahi, and his Peruvian interpreter, Victor Borja, infuriated Peruvian and Japanese authorities when they broke a police cordon on Tuesday by entering the residence from a nearby private house.
They held a two-hour meeting with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, who have been holding hostages for more than three weeks.
Police detained the pair upon their exit and have held them since. Government officials said they would soon be released.
Pandolfi added that authorities will return the confiscated videotape to TV Asahi in Tokyo.

A senior TV Asahi official in Lima said, however, there were no plans to send Hitomi out of the country. "We have not consented nor have we agreed (with police authorities on sending Hitomi out of the country)," said Tomoo Tama, the company's New York bureau chief.
A senior government source said on Friday that Peru would not exercise its right to charge Hitomi and Borja under terrorism laws, but wanted the detention to serve as an example.
"It's a matter of taking dissuasive measures," he said, adding that the detention of the men was a signal to journalists that they cannot go too far.

Increasingly irked by the huge media presence outside the residence, the Peruvian government is considering widening the exclusion zone around the building to prevent unauthorised entries and the transmission of MRTA messages.
"The media is hardly helping us," the government source said. "In fact, without them, we would be far closer to solving this."

The government maintains that the Asahi employees' action, and a previous impromptu press conference within the residence, set back negotiations and prevented the release of more hostages by denying the government an important bargaining chip of deciding when to grant the MRTA publicity.
